pll2d9c3-d1e3514.summary: Explains that the names are given not for the angels' sake but for ours; each order is named from gifts held not singularly but excellently, since in heaven nothing is possessed singularly, though some possess more sublimely. The higher orders receive all gifts more sublimely but are named from the chief ones; Seraphim, the highest, are named from charity, a greater gift than knowledge.
claims: Names are given for our sake.
All gifts are shared in heaven in different degrees.

pll2d9c3-d1e3519.summary: Adds that knowing is greater than judging, since knowledge informs judgment, so the second order, Cherubim, is named from knowledge; likewise for the others.

pll2d9c3-d1e3522.summary: States that the orders' excellence follows the excellence of gifts, though, as Gregory says, all gifts are common to all; all burn with charity and are full of knowledge, but the higher receive them more excellently and are named from them.
claims: All angels have all gifts in some degree.

pll2d9c3-d1e3540.summary: Cites Gregory: in that city each order is named from what it received more fully as gift.
claims: Each order is named for its fuller gift.

pll2d9c3-d1e3555.summary: Raises the objection: if each order is named for what it possesses more fully, Cherubim excel all in knowledge.

pll2d9c3-d1e3569.summary: Answers that whoever loves more knows more (each knows as much as he loves), so Seraphim excel also in knowledge; the comparison refers not to all orders but to the lower ones, and an order is named not from everything it has more fully but from one of them.
claims: The comparison is with lower orders.

pll2d9c3-d1e3584.summary: Alternatively the comparison refers not to other orders but to some of the order's own gifts: as humans excel in some gifts more than others, angels may too.
claims: An order may be named for its own strongest gift.

pl-l2d9c3.summary: Explains that the names are given for our sake, from gifts possessed not singularly but excellently, since in heaven nothing is held singularly, though some possess more sublimely. The higher orders have all gifts more sublimely, but take their names from the chief gifts: Seraphim from charity, greater than knowledge; Cherubim from knowledge, greater than judgment. All burn with charity and are full of knowledge (Gregory), but each order is named for what it received more fully. To the objection that then Cherubim excel all in knowledge, Lombard answers that whoever loves more knows more, so Seraphim excel in knowledge too; the comparison refers to lower orders, or to some of an order's own gifts.
claims: Angelic names are given for our sake.
In heaven all gifts are shared by all, though in different degrees.
Each order is named for a gift it has more excellently.
Charity is a greater gift than knowledge.
Whoever loves more knows more, so the Seraphim excel also in knowledge.
An order's name compares it to lower orders, not to all.
